action_criteria.expected_evidence: Compared with the EMG of 8 years ago, new active and chronic denervation in cervical muscles and new active denervation in the tongue, thoracic paraspinals and right tibialis anterior, outside the old left-leg polio distribution; no conduction block; normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No demyelinating, vascular or mass lesion; subtle corticospinal tract T2 hyperintensity, new since the MRI of 5 years ago, supportive only.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Old left-predominant atrophy of the lumbar enlargement, conus and ventral roots, unchanged; no cord compression, cord signal change, canal stenosis or root compression.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 820 U/L (4.8x ULN); blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 72% predicted and SNIP 52 cmH2O, both reduced: inspiratory muscle weakness that needs early respiratory referral.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 expansion and no pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1; a negative result does not exclude a genetic contribution.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No clinically significant interaction with hydrochlorothiazide or as-needed acetaminophen; liver-function monitoring schedule for riluzole.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. Hydrochlorothiazide and as-needed acetaminophen have no clinically significant interaction with it.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
Do not attribute the new bulbar, upper motor neuron and right-sided findings to post-polio syndrome and continue energy conservation alone.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive bilateral arm and right leg weakness with upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman signs, a right Babinski sign and a brisk jaw jerk) and lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral regions beyond the old polio distribution on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now because FVC (72% predicted) and SNIP (52 cmH2O) are already reduced; screen for orthopnoea and nocturnal hypoventilation with overnight oximetry or capnography, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.
Arrange a speech and language therapy assessment of speech and swallowing, with communication support, and monitor weight and swallowing at each review.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman signs, a right Babinski sign and a brisk jaw jerk with lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral regions, beyond the old left-leg polio distribution, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy.
CK 820 U/L (4.8x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

FVC 72% predicted and SNIP 52 cmH2O are reduced, without an AAN 2009 marker yet. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

Post-polio syndrome is new weakness, fatigue and atrophy in the muscles affected by the original polio, slowly progressive and purely lower motor neuron; upper motor neuron signs, new bulbar involvement and new denervation outside the polio distribution on comparison with the earlier EMG point to a superimposed motor neuron disease.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Post-polio syndrome is slowly progressive, lower motor neuron only and confined to the muscles affected by the original polio; new tongue atrophy, upper motor neuron signs (Hoffman, Babinski, brisk reflexes), faster progression and EMG denervation outside the polio distribution indicate a superimposed motor neuron disease.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the progressive weakness on post-polio syndrome and defers the ALS work-up

patient.history_present_illness:
Mrs. L is a 61-year-old woman with known post-polio syndrome who has experienced worsening weakness over 8 months that both she and her neurologist are concerned may represent a new process superimposed on her post-polio syndrome.

She had paralytic polio at age 8 which primarily affected her left leg. She recovered partially with residual left leg weakness and atrophy. At age 53, she developed post-polio syndrome, with new fatigue and slowly progressive weakness in her left leg. This was confirmed by EMG showing chronic polio changes (enlarged motor units) with new active changes in the left leg, and she has been managed with energy conservation and supportive care.

Over the past 8 months, however, the rate of progression has accelerated and new symptoms have emerged beyond the distribution of her original polio: bilateral arm weakness with hand atrophy, new right leg weakness not present before, tongue atrophy and fasciculations (a region never affected in her original polio), and new upper motor neuron signs (bilateral Hoffman signs, right Babinski).

Her neurologist has urgently referred her for comprehensive evaluation of these new findings.
